descriptor.scene: A close INSERT of the apartment wall: two strong bare forearms below navy polo sleeves, DAVID's hands, pinning one more small photograph onto a corkboard already crowded with dozens of little photographs of brunches, faces around tables, pancakes held up like trophies, mismatched mugs raised. Among the photos, a small hand-lettered card reads exactly thebrunchguy in lowercase marker letters, and below the board a glass jar spills a few small plain wooden tokens onto the shelf. Desk-lamp warmth. The faces in the photographs are tiny and soft, no larger than a thumbnail, none of them a recognizable canon character. Lower-right: bare shelf wood, calm.
descriptor._caption: The internet gave him a name for it. Online he is thebrunchguy, and regulars collected little brunch tokens for showing up, the way kids collect arcade tickets. When your nickname is a meal you share with strangers, you are doing something right.
negatives: any legible text besides the exact card thebrunchguy
a visible face of David (hands and forearms only)
photorealistic photographs: the pinned photos are tiny warm ink-and-wash vignettes

The output has exactly ONE camera, ONE moment, and NO internal borders, frames, gutters, or dividing lines of any kind. DIRECTION OF TRAVEL. If a person in this scene is moving toward something, that destination MUST BE AHEAD OF THEM IN THE FRAME and they must be seen FROM BEHIND or from three-quarters behind, so the viewer is following them into it. A figure whose face is toward the camera is walking AWAY from everything behind them: if the thing they are moving toward is drawn behind them, the picture says the opposite of the scene. Their feet, hips, shoulders and gaze all point the same way, along the direction of travel. A NAMED CHARACTER SITTING IN A CROWD IS STILL PART OF THAT CROWD. When someone the story cares about is among an audience, congregation, class or crowd, they FACE THE SAME WAY EVERYONE ELSE FACES and hold the same posture as the people around them. They are NOT turned out toward the camera while the rest of the room faces the speaker, NOT swivelled in their seat, NOT leaning into the aisle, NOT lit differently, NOT haloed, and NOT given more space around them than their neighbours. A figure facing a different direction from everyone around them reads as detached from the room, or as though they are looking at something nobody else can see. IF THE SCENE NEEDS THEIR FACE, MOVE THE CAMERA, NOT THE PERSON: shoot the crowd from in front or from the side so their face is naturally visible while they still face what everyone else faces. Make them findable by PLACEMENT and by what they wear, never by breaking the room's shared orientation. HANDS. Every hand in this image has EXACTLY FOUR FINGERS AND ONE THUMB, five digits and no more and no fewer, and every person has exactly TWO hands and TWO arms. No sixth finger, no extra thumb, no duplicated or spare limb, and no hand emerging from a place no arm reaches. Two hands that come near each other stay SEPARATE and readable as two hands: they never merge into one mass, never share fingers and never fuse at the knuckles. Each hand is joined to a wrist of believable thickness, the wrist to a forearm, and the forearm to the shoulder of the person it belongs to. Hands are sized to their owner: never oversized, never doll-small. A hand resting ON something makes real contact with THAT thing, with the fingers following its actual surface and not floating above it or sinking into it.
